children: The Web Demo receiver turns a publish Webhooks event into a revalidateTag call that refreshes reader pages in ~1–2 seconds.

Cache Revalidation is what happens on the consumer side of a Webhooks delivery. The Web Demo's webhook receiver verifies the HMAC signature, reads the affected Document id and type, and calls Next.js revalidateTag against the cache tags those reader pages were rendered under. The stale page is busted and re-fetched from HTTP API v1 on the next request — end to end in roughly

The demo previously relied on ISR with revalidate=300, meaning an editor's change could sit invisible for up to five minutes. Tag-based revalidation flips that from a polling timer to an event push: a Mutation's publish step fires the webhook, the webhook hits the receiver, the receiver busts exactly the tags that changed. Editors see their work near-instantly, and pages that didn't change keep their cache.

This closes the loop that begins at Mutation, travels through Webhooks signing and dedup, and lands at the Web Demo reader. It is the realtime delivery contract for Barkpark content and the reason the JS SDK consumer can trust a published change is visible quickly. On the Barkpark side, the revalidation fan-out is dispatched as background work by an Oban Worker rather than inline on the write — so a slow or briefly-down receiver never stalls the publish. That async-delivery posture is part of Operations' broader rule that a write on one surface ripples consistently to every other.
